text: Good afternoon. I am pleased to call to order this Albuquerque County Board of Supervisors meeting on the 5th of November at 1 p.m. in Lane Auditorium. I'd like to note at the dais we have Supervisor Ann Malick of the Whitehall District, Supervisor Ned Galloway of the Ryo District, Supervisor Diantha McKeel of the Jack DeWitt District, Supervisor B. Lupisto-Curtley of the Ravenna District, and Supervisor Mike Pruitt of the Scottsville District, myself, Jim Andrews, representing the Samuel Miller District.

A quorum is present. And we are also joined by our county executive, Mr. Jeff Richardson, county attorney, Mr. Andy Herrick, and our clerk, Ms. Claudette Borgerson. Also, let me please welcome and introduce Albemarle County police officers present, Sergeant Jason Freistad and Master Police Officer Dana.

Oh, no, not Dana. It's so many. I'm not sure. Dana's not here. Anyway, we thank you both for your service today and every day on behalf of the constituents of Albemarle County and for our safety and security.
If all present could now stand as you are able and join us in the Pledge of Allegiance. And to the Republic for which it stands, one nation, under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.
Thank you. If you please join us for a moment of silence.

Board, our first business course is to adopt the final agenda. I have not heard of any suggested changes. If there is a motion to approve the final agenda. So moved. Second. We have a motion from Supervisor McKeel. Second from Supervisor Malek. Without objection, call the roll.

My news is that last Wednesday I attended the Rural Center of Virginia's conference. It was in Hanover, and there were quite a few excellent presentations and the notes and materials I will share with board and staff.

But Jason Alcuda, Juan Pablo Segura from the Virginia Economic Development Department talked about how to protect rural lands and the rural businesses which live there and to spread some of the benefits of our economic growth to long-established rural businesses and also new ones who might come. But people mentioned about how important it is that the environmental protection that many counties have actually is a benefit and telling the story of the culture that

your county has is a way to make sure that the companies who work there and or want to come there actually see their the culture of the receiving community as a fit and to see how they will fit in the rural urban interface is also while it's a problem it's also an asset because in the urban areas you have lots of customers and in the rural area you have lots of producing land So that can be made to be a benefit, but we all have to work diligently and carefully to facilitate those kinds of exchanges.

And back in 2010, the program to get farm-to-table or farmers directly to consumers was very much a regional effort, and we're living in the benefits of many of those things now. talked about economic development and the wide variety of different county levels.

Some have zero staff. I thought about the fact that until about 2013, Admiral County's philosophy was the University of Virginia will take care of all of our economic development and we don't have to. And it was through the efforts organizing of the board, actually from 2010 to 2014, that began to put more of a focus on that.

One of the leaders' comments that stayed with me forever was a good job or a better job is a wonderful way to solve the housing affordability problem. So it's one of the many assets that we have, and it certainly helped me to figure out how I fit in.

They talked about the AFID program, the agricultural investments that our county also has used. So I was very proud to be thinking that Albemarle has been using these resources and these state programs to great benefit for our local citizens, and I hope that we will continue.

And I'm zooming down here. The last program was about historic preservation tax credits and how many communities have used them to tremendous benefit to restore or repurpose old buildings. There's a river block in Danville, and the owner was there with his designer and also a funding advisor person talking about the assets that they have created in eight properties all along one street and the tremendous return to the citizens and the community from that.

So anyway, that's my report. Thank you very much. Thank you. Supervisor Galloway. Yes, thank you. I'd like to just, I mean, we had an election yesterday. I also want to thank there was a competitive race for school board in the Rio District. Leslie Pryor, who was appointed this past few months ago, the start of the year, and Jim Dillenbeck were the candidates. So I thank both of them for running for school board

and stepping up to run, as we all know, has its challenges. So I appreciate that they did so. And congratulate Mr. Dillenbeck on a successful candidacy as he was voted in to represent RIO come the start of the next year. I had a chance to visit and go inside and see the operations at three of the five in the RIO district.

As always, we have got one hell of a volunteer team that run elections in this county. They know what they're doing. They know the rules. They're pleasant. So everything was going smoothly. They all had the data. They understood how early voting impacted it. So it was just really nice to see and visit with those folks and see kind of behind the scenes what was happening in those three particular precincts, but thank them for volunteer efforts to make sure we had safe and successful elections.

The other part that I'd like to note is that we have two political parties often set up at all of our precincts around the county. And with all the ones I visited yesterday, as has been the case in the past, you've got Republicans and Democrats there all being cordial and respectful and having lovely dialogue with one another.

I sometimes wish our federal and state politicians would come down and see what that means and what that looks like. Because, you know, a gust of wind would come, and it didn't matter whose sample ballots went flying over the parking lot. Everybody scurried from their tent to help pick them up. So they all understand what it takes to be out there.

So I'm grateful to the citizens who volunteered being out there advocating for their political opinions, but doing so in a way that was both courteous and respectful of the voters that are coming through but to one another and not allowing any sort of partisan divide. They were out there volunteering and doing it in a lovely way.

I suspect that is the case around the whole county because I've heard that and I've even seen it years ago when I had to run countywide. That was what I witnessed as well. So just very appreciative to all those involved and who put the time out there. It was a lovely day. And, you know, the results, I'm sure some people are happy with the results.

Some people aren't. But at the end of the day, that's how it works. But the process to get there was well done at Albemarle, and I'm very grateful for that. So thank you. Thank you. Supervisor LePistro-Krutman. Well, and piggybacking on that, we also have newly elected two new supervisors, although we are going to be very sad to see Diantha and Jim leave.
We want to congratulate Sally Duncan and Fred Missel on their win. So they'll be, yes. So thank you. And this morning I was at the topping out ceremony at Center 2 at Abelmoral High School.

And lastly, I know I'm going to step on Mike's toes, but we have Veterans Day coming up November the 11th. And at 11 o'clock, we will have a ceremony here in the county office building. and you you all are invited this is something very special where all veterans get honored and uh this is something dear near and dear to all of our hearts and so we encourage you to come that's all thank you thank you uh supervisor pruitt thank you you know everyone has to have a little bit of a ball uh hand on the ball with uh election day congratulations so i would um

additionally like to extend a congratulations to molly angbein who won a seat on scottsville Town Council in a surprise election, right? And in doing so, unseated Eddie Payne. And so I'd really like to extend my thanks to Councillor Payne for his years of selfless service to the town of Scottsville. And I look forward to working with the new Councillor. I'd also like to recognize Councillor Gritzko in the audience. Thank you for joining us today. Additionally, as we've already heard, Commissioner Fred Missel has won a seat and is now Supervisor-elect Fred Missal that means we need a new Scottsville Planning Commissioner and I am

already thinking about it and if anyone knows anyone who would be interested in this I would love to chat with people because this is probably the most consequential appointment that any supervisor gets to make and I get the privilege of making one twice because of the incredible success of Fred Missal now I should also bear mention we haven't really talked about the top of the ticket I do think it matters because it's something we talk about in this board very frequently, right? Governor Youngkin has been an ally of this county at times on economic development issues. He has helped us significantly, and we've worked well with him.

But there are other ways in which Governor Youngkin has provided roadblocks for really important county priorities. He has vetoed funding initiatives that were specifically earmarked for our county, and he has blocked things that we've identified as our highest priority pieces of legislation. I am really optimistic for what the new administration might spell for some of our specific high-priority issues, and I hope that we have a continued and even stronger working relationship with the new administration, because I think there's a lot of new movement that we can make. Getting off the election, I should mention the Scottsville School and Hickory Hope in

Southwood, both in the Scottsville district, right? These both, they are complicated to get seats in, to be a resident of, because you have to apply for a government lottery that is administered locally, and those wait lists aren't normally open. They are about to open. So on the 7th of November until the 14th of November, the wait list for the Scottsville school and for Hickory Hope in the Scottsville district will be open. If you are a low-income qualifying resident, I would encourage people to apply.

This is really one of the best deals you can get. It is really reliable, low-income housing and two of the best communities that we have in all of Albemarle County. And feel free to reach out to anyone in the county about how that – if you want to reach out to me, I will put you in contact with the right people, please.

Additionally, I should mention that there are some significant consequences that face our community with the federal shutdown. The most immediate that I know people are concerned about is SNAP. There are 3,000 people in the county, roughly, who rely on SNAP. The state is stepping in to provide stopgap funding, but it is going to be on a different basis than normal.

This is a state-administered program, not local, and they are going to be doing it in one-week-at-a-time increments. So please be aware, members of the community, that that is how your SNAP benefits are going to be being rolled out presently. But there should be a relative non-interruption in services. You just might have to buy your groceries on a weekly basis rather than a monthly basis.

Additionally, people who are on vouchers, if you receive a housing choice voucher either in a project-based context, such as the Scottsville School, or if you're in some other private marketplace where you're using a Section 8 housing choice voucher, the government is not going to be paying their portion of it anymore.

You still have to continue to pay your portion, but the government will not pay their portion. This is also very important because your landlord is not allowed to evict you for the government not paying their portion. And so I would encourage anyone who is facing issues with their landlord during the government funding freeze to make sure you both notify your voucher administrator here in the county and also reach out to legal aid.

Legal Aid Justice Center and Central Virginia Legal Aid will both be able to help people who are facing illegal evictions for the government's nonpayment of their rent portion. And finally, I should just mention there was an incident at UVA over the last few days.

Blanking on it, I want to say it was on Sunday. No, I'm thinking the active shooter incident, right? There was not an actual active shooter, but there was a warning of it. and it was something that I realized I felt so much closer than I have in the past, right?

I was actually, you know, a UVA student during one of the last really significant incidents, but it didn't touch me in a personal way. But this time there was a threat at Shannon Library. I have a person who works for me who is a current UVA student, and I reached out to her immediately, and I learned that she was at Shannon Library.

She had to be evacuated. She had to sprint across the lawn under guard of police officers to get to a new shelter-in-place location. She was cool as a cucumber about it, took it in stride, but I don't know.

I'm not a father. But it hit me in a very different way than these incidents have in the past, and it reminded me just what a chilling situation this is. Yet another false report of the type I had hoped to figure out how we can legislate solutions to combat here in the commonwealth and and just such a it brings home the kind of personal impacts that parents in this community feel every single day i know when we have these kinds of incidents in our schools and it to me really highlighted the importance of figuring out what the hell we're doing well

that's all i have thank you and all i will add is that i also appreciate how well the elections were run yesterday and observed locally went off without a minor hitches but nothing that couldn't be readily overcome and you know and with professionalism and grace by everybody i very appreciative of the candidates and congratulate fred missal who'll be taking my place on the board and i will promise to try to make that transition as smooth as possible for for the benefit of all. The magisterial districts that have new supervisors coming on will be advertising new positions and needing some folks to step up to the plate to apply for those positions.

The Planning Commission is one, but there are other commissions as well, boards and commissions, the service authorities. So if you're interested in serving, especially in the Samuel Miller and the Jack Jewett, I think Ryo, you're in good shape as far as you're going to handle your own.

But those that are turning over, many of those boards and commissions will be advertised. So if people are interested, they should take a look at the county website and see what's open and available and consider applying to serve your community.

Thank you, Mike, for mentioning it. I appreciate it. May I add one thing? Sure. At the election yesterday, I was surprised to hear both at Earliesville Precincts and Free Union that quite a few in the dozens of long-time frequent voter individuals, long-time residents had been purged and that they were able to work this out it was a sort of that oh my god sort of initial shock was surprising but the staff in both places was able to smooth this over with

the provisional ballot and go through all that stuff again but it does remind me that all of us need to before the election go and check and make sure that we have not been erased in some way so I was very surprised to hear that. But thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

Board, next up is proclamations and recognitions, and I believe that Professor Pruitt will read a proclamation as a motion. Thank you, Chair. Whereas, throughout our nation's history, the United States of America has called on its citizens in uniform to serve and protect our national security, and whereas, at home and abroad, generations of American patriots have defended the freedom and American values of equality, democracy, and justice for all.

And whereas November 11th, 2025 marks the 87th anniversary of Veterans Day being recognized as a national holiday. On this day and every day, we remember the millions of patriots who have served and sacrificed for the betterment of our nation. And whereas many veterans continue to serve their country in public schools and government as public officials, teachers, police officer, fire and rescue, and other professions providing service to all community members.

And whereas, with a profound debt of gratitude, we especially recognize the local veterans in Albemarle County for their continued service. Now, therefore, be it proclaimed that we, the Albemarle County Board of Supervisors, do hereby recognize November 11th as Veterans Day and celebrate all who have served our country around the world and continue to serve as veterans in Albemarle County signed this day, the 5th of November, 2025.

Second. We have a motion from Supervisor Pruitt. Second from Supervisor McKeel. Without objection, a clerk will call the roll. Ms. McKeel? Yes. Mr. Pruitt? Aye. Mr. Andrews? Yes. Mr. Galloway? Yes. Ms. Lapista-Kirtley? Aye. Ms. Malik? Yes.

I'd like to introduce Kai. As a fellow veteran, he was commissioned through Officer Candidate School in February of 1995, completed Nuclear Power School in March of 1996. He reported to the USS John C. Stennis, CVN-74, as Reactor's Control Division officer.

The Stennis is a Nimitz-class carrier, or as us submariners call it, a very big target. He earned his propulsion watch officer and surface warfare designations while at the Stennis. He left active duty in 2000.

Captain Maori transitioned to the Naval Reserve, where he served in a variety of operational and leadership roles. His assignment included mobilization to the Joint Task Force Guantanamo and Airy Support Group Kuwait, as well as key billets with U.S. Fleet Forces Command, Second Fleet, Sixth Fleet, Carrier Strike Group 4, concluded his career serving as a commanding officer of the Reserve Board of Inspection and Survey Unit.

Captain Mowry retired in 2022 after 28 years of distinguished service, and he joined us shortly thereafter. It's been an honor to work with Kai and see his leadership and his great experience have a positive impact in public works and for our community.

And so with that, I'll introduce Kai. Thank you. Thank you. Welcome, Captain Mowry. Thank you for being here. I promise, it's short. Good afternoon, Chair Andrews, Vice Chair McKeel, members of the board, fellow citizens.

It is an honor to accept this proclamation on behalf of the proud veterans of Albemarle County. As you know, my name is Kai Mowry, and I currently serve as the Deputy Chief of Operations for Facilities and Environmental Services. I retired after 28 years of service as a captain in the United States Navy.

I know firsthand the deep sense of duty, sacrifice, and pride that comes with serving our nation. This proclamation is more than just words on paper. It is a meaningful recognition of the generations of men and women who have defended our freedoms, both at home and abroad.

It reminds us that Veterans Day is not just a date on the calendar, but a moment to reflect on the values of equality, democracy, and justice that so many have fought to protect. I accept this on behalf of all local veterans, those who continue to serve our community as teachers, first responders, public servants, and neighbors.

We are proud to call Albemarle County home, and we are grateful for your continued support and recognition. Thank you for honoring our service and for standing with us, not just on Veterans Day, but every day. Thank you very much. If you will remain for a moment, I'm sure that supervisors will want to express their appreciation for veterans in the form of different comments.

Supervisor McKeel? Sure. Thank you for being here today, for working for the county, and for your service. I'm always amazed in my life in Albemarle County how many veterans we have in Albemarle County.

There are a huge number, whether it's at the University of Virginia or Albemarle County or the city, and certainly veterans that have just retired to our area, and they really are so beneficial and just make a really important contribution to our community.

I will remind folks, and I think Bea mentioned it, that on Tuesday we have a veterans ceremony in recognition in this building, in the auditorium. It starts at 11 o'clock, and I also am aware that there are other veterans celebrations around the county.

Thank you very much. Yes, thank you for being here. What was the nuclear science piece again? What was that, the school? It's Naval Nuclear Power School. During the time set up for public comment on matters previously considered or currently pending before the board, individuals may address the Board of Supervisors. Individuals are allowed one opportunity of up to three minutes to speak at each board meeting.

A sign-up sheet is managed by the clerk's office. Timekeeping is conducted through a timer and light system at the podium. The green light will go on when you begin speaking, which begins your allotted time. The yellow light indicates you have one minute to finish speaking. The red light indicates your time has expired, and you will be asked to end your comments.

In order to give all speakers equal treatment and courtesy, the board requests that speakers adhere to the following guidelines. When addressing the board, state your name and if you live in Albemarle County, your magisterial district. Address comments directly to the board as a whole. Any written statements or other supporting material may be given to the clerk.

If representing a group or organization, you may ask others present to raise their hands in recognition. Speakers may not share any unused time with another speaker. Back-and-forth debate is not permitted, and do not speak from your seat or out of turn. All comments are live-streamed, recorded, and published on the Elmar County website.

Supervisors, when the tornado hit the cheese factory and the reporters went there, can you guess what the report was? The reporter said debris was everywhere.

You can be thankful that as a bad dad joke teller, that'll be my only joke. What I have to share with you, though, is much more important. There's a really amazing moment in history that we can remember.

Very soon, in fact, imminently, there'll be a new statue in the United States Capitol honoring Barbara Johns. This young woman who did this courageous act, she gave an incredible speech on April the 23rd, 1951.

In fact, our governor-elect last night, this is what she said about it as she was recounting Virginia history. She said, where Washington and Jefferson established a government by and for the people, it was also where Barbara Johns, a 16-year-old girl from Farmville, led a walkout of students that would be part of Brown v. Board of Education.

Barbara Johns never gave up, and she showed us that no matter what age, you can be part of the change and the progress here in Virginia and across the nation. Supervisors, in my job, I work in the tour industry, and I've had the honor of doing a lot of presentations about Virginia history.
